title: TTHE: Test-Time Harness Evolution
abstract:
The behavior of an LLM agent is determined not only by the underlying model, but also by its harness: the executable program that constructs context, invokes tools, verifies intermediate results, and recovers from failures. Existing approaches typically optimize harnesses on training or development data and freeze the resulting programs at test time, limiting adaptation to shifts in task distributions, failure modes, and tool interactions. We ask whether the harness can instead be optimized during evaluation using unlabeled execution traces. We introduce Test-Time Harness Evolution (TTHE), which treats the executable harness as the state of test-time adaptation. On each unlabeled test batch, TTHE iteratively evolves a population of candidate harnesses through agentic proposers that reason over execution traces and explore diverse edit directions. A judge selects a candidate using execution traces and execution-derived proxy signals.

The selected harness determines the current batch's outputs and initializes adaptation on the next. Crucially, the solver, proposers, and judge operate through different harnesses around the same frozen LLM, without weight updates, access to final-answer labels, or a separately trained adaptation model. Across six execution-grounded benchmarks spanning text-to-SQL, competitive programming, software engineering, data-science coding, terminal-based tasks, and agentic tool use, TTHE improves fixed ReAct-style baseline harnesses through persistent, inspectable * Corresponding authors. Code: https://github.com/junnie00/TTHE program adaptation. These results recast test-time adaptation for LLM agents as evolution over executable control programs and identify execution-derived proxy reliability as a central challenge for robust unsupervised agent improvement.

sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
Modern LLM agents are increasingly built as executable systems rather than single-call predictors. Their behavior depends not only on the model, but also on the executable harness around it-the control program that constructs context, invokes tools, verifies intermediate results, and implements recovery strategies. Following prior work on model and agent harnesses [Lee et al., 2026, Zhang et al., 2026a], we focus on this program as the object of adaptation. Its context construction and control flow determine how the model's capabilities are used. A common development workflow, however, is to inspect failures, adjust prompts and control flow, and tune tool-use logic before evaluating the resulting harness as a fixed artifact. Its operating procedure then remains unchanged even when the target workload exposes different requirements or failure modes. This convention treats evaluation as a scoring stage, even though execution itself produces rich operational evidence. Every attempted task leaves an execution trace: model calls, tool actions, intermediate outputs, database responses, test results, runtime errors, and recovery decisions. Such traces can reveal not only whether an execution satisfies available checks, but also how its operating procedure might be improved. A text-to-SQL agent may retrieve the correct table but apply an inconsistent value normalization; a coding agent may generate plausible patches without verifying them before submission; a data-science agent may compute an intermediate result but omit it from the final report. This is precisely the kind of evidence a human harness engineer would inspect when revising the scaffold. Crucially, this evidence is available during evaluation without access to gold labels.

Using this evidence to revise the harness, however, is different from using it to refine individual responses. Self-debugging and reflection use feedback to revise candidate answers or retain textual experience for later attempts [Chen et al., 2024, Shinn et al., 2023]. Automated prompt and workflow search targets the surrounding task-solving procedure, but typically optimizes it against a training or development objective before evaluating the resulting workflow as a fixed artifact [Khattab et al., 2023, Hu et al., 2025, Zhang et al., 2025b]. More recent work revises agent source code, harnesses, and configurations using execution feedback or task-level evaluation signals [Cai et al., 2026a, Lee et al., 2026, Zhang et al., 2026a, He et al., 2025]. Building on these lines of work, we ask: can an LLM agent adapt its harness at test time using its own execution traces, without final correctness feedback?

We propose Test-Time Harness Evolution (TTHE), which treats the executable harness as the state of test-time adaptation. Rather than searching for a harness on labeled development instances and freezing it for evaluation, TTHE moves harness optimization into the evaluation process itself. On each unlabeled test batch, TTHE executes a population of candidate harnesses and iteratively refines them through traceguided proposers that explore diverse edit directions. A judge selects one candidate using the traces and execution-derived proxy signals; the selected harness determines the current batch's outputs and initializes adaptation on the next. Final correctness feedback is used only for post-selection evaluation. The solver, proposers, and judge use the same frozen LLM in different roles, so adaptation changes the executable program rather than model weights and requires no separately trained adaptation model. This evaluation-time formulation offers two practical advantages. First, it adapts at the point where the relevant evidence appears: after the agent encounters the schemas, repositories, tests, tools, and runtime constraints of the target workload. It can therefore use task-specific execution evidence without requiring an additional labeled development set tailored to that workload. Second, updating an executable program requires no gradient access and permits explicit changes to context construction, multi-sample generation, tool-mediated grounding, deterministic contract checks, and conditional recovery branches. These changes alter the procedure used to solve tasks rather than only revising an individual response.

A central challenge, however, is that execution evidence is not a correctness oracle. A query can execute successfully while answering the wrong question; code can pass visible tests while failing hidden ones. TTHE therefore presents proxy signals together with candidate code and the underlying execution traces, allowing proposers and the judge to interpret these signals in the context of how an outcome was produced rather than relying on a single surrogate score. Because an edit intended to repair a failure can also disrupt previously correct behavior, we complement this design with a conditional analysis of a class of tracetriggered harness edits, characterizing when corrective gains outweigh unintended regressions.

We evaluate TTHE on six execution-grounded benchmarks, where it improves fixed ReAct-style baselines and yields inspectable grounding, verification, and recovery policies. On the evaluated BIRD dataset, TTHE achieves 48.7% mean execution accuracy over three runs, compared with 12.7% for the fixed baseline. A separate ten-run execution-result consistencyvoting control achieves 16.0%. Harnesses selected by DeepSeek for each BIRD batch also improve MiMo V2.5 and GPT-5.5 over their respective fixedharness baselines on the corresponding batches, without further harness evolution. These results provide evidence of cross-model transfer of the evolved tasksolving procedures. Search diagnostics reveal nonmonotonic effects of search budget and distinguish candidate-availability limitations from selection errors. Together, these findings support executable harness adaptation as a practical path to test-time selfevolution in LLM agents.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text:
• We introduce Test-Time Harness Evolution (TTHE), a framework that recasts test-time adaptation as evolution over executable control programs. TTHE enables an LLM agent to transform its own execution experience into harness updates, without modifying model weights or accessing final correctness feedback.

• We demonstrate gains on evaluated tasks across six execution-grounded benchmarks, compare TTHE with fixed-harness repeated sampling on BIRD, and show that batch-specific evolved harnesses can benefit other execution models on the corresponding tasks.

sections.heading: Harness as adaptation state
sections.text:
The adaptation state is the task harness's source, including its prompts and executable control logic. TTHE revises how the harness constructs context, invokes tools, validates intermediate results, and recovers from failures, while keeping the model and the outer proposal-and-selection procedure fixed. The baseline H 0 is a ReAct-style scaffold [Yao et al., 2023], fixed before evolution begins.

A code edit can change a prompt, introduce a database probe before generation, add a deterministic output check, or create a conditional repair branch. It can also implement multiple-sample generation and aggregation [Wang et al., 2023] or execution-based selfdebugging [Chen et al., 2024]. The search is therefore not confined to choosing among predeclared prompt templates or workflow settings. The distinction from response-level refinement is the object of the update: a revised query is an output, whereas a new rule for constructing and checking queries changes the procedure applied to the batch.

sections.heading: Evolution and Selection
sections.text:
Let H g r denote branch g after round r, with H g 0 = H t for all g. The loop uses three operators under the information constraints in Section 2:

Observe(H, X t ) executes harness H on every input in X t and records its execution traces, proxy signals, and cached outcomes.

Propose(A, T ) receives the active branches A and their execution records T . One coding-agent proposer per branch revises its own parent, using the active branches' code and traces for context, and returns one child.

Judge(F, T , X t ) inspects the eligible candidates' code and signals. During selection, it may acquire additional evidence through probes or candidate re-execution, then commits one harness from F .

At the start of a batch, the incoming harness is observed once, and its cached execution record is shared across the initial branches. In each round, valid children replace their parents and are executed on X t ; invalid or unloadable children leave their parents and cached records unchanged. Two design choices organize these updates. Lineage: a fixed parent-child sequence allows successive edits to build on the branch's grounding, verification, and recovery routines. Diversity: conservative-repair, exploratory, and adversarial proposer roles encourage different edit directions. Branches can use one another's execution evidence while retaining their own lineages. After R rounds, the judge selects one harness from F t = {H g R } G g=1 based on the candidates' code, execution traces, and proxy signals. The selected harness's cached outcomes determine the current batch's score in Eq. 2, and the harness initializes adaptation on the next batch.

The solver, proposers, and judge share the same frozen LLM. The solver runs within the evolving task harness, while the proposers and judge use a Claude Code scaffold for file access, code editing, execution, and prob-ing, with all model calls routed to the same backbone.

sections.heading: THEORETICAL ANALYSIS
sections.text: We analyze a class of trace-triggered harness edits on the current batch, rather than the outer proposal-andselection process. As conditional analyses of test-time training relate an auxiliary update to the main-task objective [Sun et al., 2020], this analysis relates corrective edits to regressions.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.text:
We evaluate TTHE on six execution-grounded benchmarks: BIRD [Li et al., 2023], LiveCodeBench [Jain et al., 2025], SWE-bench Verified [Jimenez et al., 2024], DS-1000 [Lai et al., 2023], Terminal-Bench 2.1, and claw-eval. These cover text-to-SQL, competitive programming, software engineering, data-science coding, terminal-based tasks, and agentic tool use. We use fixed evaluation sets, including hard task subsets selected before adaptation; their sizes and construction procedures are given in Appendix A.

We compare each task's fixed baseline harness with TTHE initialized from that harness, using deepseek-v4-flash as the frozen solver, proposer, and judge. Following Section 2, TTHE adapts to each unlabeled batch; final correctness feedback is used only to evaluate committed outputs. Metrics are task success rates for the five binary benchmarks and mean graded scores for claw-eval. Both methods are run three times per evaluation set. Figure 2 shows the means; individual results and mean ± sample standard deviation appear in Appendix H.

sections.heading: Main Results
sections.text:
TTHE outperforms the fixed baseline on all six benchmarks in each of the three reported runs (Figure 2; Appendix H). Mean success rates increase by 8.0-36.0 percentage points on the five binary benchmarks; claweval gains 20.5 points on its 0-100 graded-score scale.

sections.heading: Ablation Studies
sections.text:
We examine repeated sampling, search configuration, cross-batch initialization, and backbone variation on BIRD. Unless stated otherwise, the ablations and further analyses below use the main experiment's BIRD subset and deepseek-v4-flash, reporting single-run accuracy separately from the three-run main results. The reference run achieves 12.0% with the fixed baseline and 50.0% with TTHE.

Repeated sampling without evolution. We run the fixed baseline ten times per question and vote over execution-result groups rather than SQL strings. This matches TTHE's nominal 1 + GR = 10 harness executions for G = 3, R = 3: one initial execution and up to nine candidate executions. Total computation also depends on harness-specific token and tool use, as well as TTHE's proposal and judging overhead. Voting raises accuracy from 12.0% to 16.0%, versus TTHE's 50.0% (Table 1). The contrast is between obtaining more outputs from an unchanged procedure and adapting the procedure that produces and checks them. The tested voting strategy does not substitute for the complete harness-evolution process.

Search budget. Search breadth and depth interact (Table 2). Increasing G from one to three does not improve accuracy at R = 1 (46.0% versus 44.0%), but improves it at R = 3 (40.0% versus 50.0%). Moreover, G = 3, R = 1 and G = 1, R = 3 allocate the same nominal number of proposals per batch but achieve 44.0% and 40.0%, respectively. These observations suggest that search organization matters beyond proposal count, with G = 3, R = 3 the best tested setting. The branch configurations combine different search widths with branch-specific proposer roles. The non-monotonic results show that supplying more evidence per update is not uniformly beneficial under this batch-level commitment rule.

Cross-batch accumulation. Resetting to the baseline before each batch achieves 44.0% accuracy, compared with 12.0% for the fixed baseline. Carrying the selected harness forward further improves overall accuracy to 50.0% (Table 3). These results indicate that current-batch adaptation yields substantial gains, while retaining evolved program structure provides a useful initialization for subsequent adaptation.

Backbone variation. We repeat evolution on BIRD with MiMo V2.5 and Kimi K2.5, using the same backbone across solver, proposer, and judge within each run (B = 10, G = 3, R = 3). Both improve over their own fixed-harness baselines: MiMo V2.5 increases from 32.0% to 52.0%, and Kimi K2.5 from 28.0% to 48.0% (Table 4). These within-model gains extend the evidence beyond the main backbone.

sections.heading: Further Analysis
sections.text:
Cross-model harness transfer. Executing DeepSeek's selected harness on the corresponding BIRD batch, without further evolution, improves MiMo V2.5 from 32.0% to 56.0% and GPT-5.5 from 36.0% to 68.0% (Table 5). Backbone variation tests The oracle over all evaluated candidates, including earlier rounds, reaches 70.0%, six points above the finalpool oracle. Both oracles use the candidate pools of the realized run. The fourteen-point gap between the judge and the final-pool oracle exceeds the six-point gain from admitting earlier candidates, highlighting selection among already generated programs as a major source of lost performance.

What strategies emerge through evolution? Inspection of the evolved harnesses reveals concrete strategies for acquiring evidence, directing repairs, and coordinating tool use. On BIRD, an evolved harness probes database values before SQL generation, grounds filter values in their stored casing, and infers the required output shape from the question. Structural violations, execution errors, and output-shape mismatches are returned as targeted feedback for subsequent attempts (Figure 4). Generation is therefore coupled with explicit checks and failure-specific revision, rather than repeated without diagnosing the preceding attempt. On SWE-bench, an evolved harness adopts a reproduce-first workflow with root-cause localization, post-edit verification, and execution of existing tests, alongside an increased step budget. It also adds a recovery branch triggered when the initial rollout returns an empty patch. This branch supplies concrete starter commands and a reproduction template, turning the absence of a usable artifact into an explicit condition for changing the execution strategy (Figure 5). The harness thus addresses not only how to verify a patch, but also how to resume execution when the agent fails to produce one. On LiveCodeBench, an evolved policy uses a low-cost path by default and escalates to additional verification and repair after a public-test failure. In claw-eval, the evolved instructions address how information and actions are linked across services. They specify single-line tool payloads, service chaining through exact identifiers rather than display names, and a pre-delivery completeness check requiring citations of retrieved record identifiers. They also require reported actions to be supported by executed tool calls. Across these examples, evolution changes what evidence the agent obtains before acting, which observations trigger revision, and how execution proceeds after failure. Execution experience is incorporated into the rules governing task solving, rather than used only to correct an individual answer.

sections.heading: LIMITATIONS
sections.text: TTHE demonstrates the potential of harness selfevolution without final task-correctness supervision. However, the feedback guiding evolution remains limited by the informativeness of execution traces and partial checks. Successful execution or agreement among candidates can coexist with semantic errors, making it difficult to distinguish effective program improvements from changes that merely satisfy available proxies. Our diagnostics show that useful candidates can already exist in the search pool yet remain unselected. This highlights a central challenge: an agent must draw on its own experience both to identify promising changes and to assess whether those changes constitute genuine progress. Developing principled mechanisms for extracting more informative feedback, guiding program exploration, and selecting beneficial updates while preserving useful behavior remains an important direction for advancing reliable unsupervised agent self-evolution.

sections.heading: CONCLUSION
sections.text: TTHE turns test-time execution experience into updates to an agent's executable harness, without changing model weights or accessing final correctness feedback during adaptation. Across six executiongrounded benchmarks, it improves over fixed baseline harnesses on the evaluated task sets and produces inspectable grounding, verification, and recovery poli-cies. Transfer experiments further show that batchspecific evolved harnesses can benefit other execution models on the corresponding tasks. Our conditional analysis characterizes the balance between corrective gains and unintended regressions for trace-triggered edits, while search diagnostics show that generating useful candidates does not ensure that they are selected. Together, these findings support executable harness adaptation as a practical path to test-time self-evolution, with reliable selection under incomplete evidence remaining a central challenge.

sections.heading: B DISCOVERED HARNESS POLICIES
sections.text:
The evolved programs are retained as source code rather than summarized only by aggregate scores. Recurring discovered policies include:

• Text-to-SQL: value grounding through database probes, date-format repair, explicit output-shape checks, and removal of accidental limits on list queries.

• LiveCodeBench: multiple candidate programs, execution-based ranking on public tests, targeted repair from expected-versus-observed outputs, and fresh-start recovery after repeated failure.

• SWE-bench: reproduce-first debugging, root-cause localization before editing, post-edit verification, and an anti-paralysis failsafe for issues that would otherwise return an empty patch (Figure 5).

• DS-1000: insertion-only output contracts, deterministic self-checks, and guards against redefining supplied variables.

• claw-eval: single-line tool payloads so write actions are recorded, per-record identifier citation with a predelivery completeness check, exact-identifier service chaining, and a prohibition on reporting unexecuted actions (see the claw-eval section below).

These policies are examples of program-level adaptation: they modify the control procedure used across instances rather than appending a one-off answer correction. It grounds filter values against the database for exact casing, infers the expected output shape from the question, and wraps generation in an execute-and-self-debug loop that returns each failure a targeted error message-structural check, execution error, empty result, wrong column count-before a final shape fix. The baseline is a standard ReAct harness (before any test-time evolution).

sections.heading: C THE CLAW-EVAL AGENTIC TOOL-USE DOMAIN
sections.text:
C.1 Task, metric, and protocol claw-eval tasks are multi-service office workflows: the solver reads mail, searches a knowledge base, looks up contacts, inspects a CRM or helpdesk, schedules meetings, and updates tickets through tool calls. The score is a per-task graded rubric in [0, 1], rather than binary execution accuracy. Each rubric combines completion, robustness, and communication criteria under a safety factor; a held-out model grader assesses the committed behavior.

The 30 tasks come from 139 agentic tasks: we retain the 112 served entirely by local deterministic mock services, then select those on which the frozen baseline scores below 0.60. The solver is deepseek-v4-flash inside the OpenClaw agent, and the proposer edits its system prompt and skills as source code. The run processes the tasks in six batches, evolving one general harness from the baseline. The grader is disabled during in-loop observation, so no task score or rubric target enters the proposer or judge; gold grading is applied only to the committed harness for measurement. The baseline and TTHE scores, 48.9% and 69.4%, are each averaged over three runs (Appendix H). The tasks are ordered by ascending baseline difficulty, so this evaluation does not isolate the effect of cross-batch accumulation.

sections.heading: C.2 Discovered policies
sections.text: From label-free traces alone the accumulated harness adds four general rules to the baseline: single-line tool payloads for reliable action capture; citation of every retrieved record identifier under a completeness checklist before delivery; chaining services by exact identifier (email or ID) rather than display name; and grounding every reported action in an executed tool call.

sections.heading: D RELATED WORK
sections.text:
Prompt and workflow optimization. Research on optimizing the system around a language model spans instructions, workflows, and executable programs. APE and OPRO search for instructions [Zhou et al., 2023, Yang et al., 2024a], while Promptbreeder and EvoPrompt use evolutionary prompt optimization [Fernando et al., 2024, Guo et al., 2024]. DSPy optimizes declarative language-model pipelines against a metric [Khattab et al., 2023]; ADAS and AFlow extend the search to agent designs and code-represented workflows [Hu et al., 2025, Zhang et al., 2025b]. FunSearch illustrates the broader potential of executable program search [Romera-Paredes et al., 2024]. More recently, GEPA uses natural-language reflection on reasoning and tool-use trajectories to propose prompt updates and combine complementary improvements from a Pareto frontier [Agrawal et al., 2026]. Thus, interpreting execution traces is already an important optimization mechanism; TTHE studies its use for revising and selecting an executable harness on the current test batch without final task-correctness feedback.

Executable harness evolution. A related line modifies agent source code or accumulates executable components. STOP and the Darwin Gödel Machine revise agent scaffolds [Zelikman et al., 2023, Zhang et al., 2025a], Voyager builds a reusable skill library [Wang et al., 2024], and MOSS studies source-level rewriting from failure trajectories [Cai et al., 2026a]. Among harness-level methods, Self-Harness validates edits through verifier-grounded evaluation and regression tests with a fixed model [Zhang et al., 2026a]; Meta-Harness gives its proposer access to historical code, scores, and traces from a search set before held-out evaluation [Lee et al., 2026]. HarnessX provides composable harness primitives and a trace-driven multi-agent evolution engine, with both harness-only adaptation and a harness-model co-evolution loop that reuses trajectories for model training [Chen et al., 2026]. HASE unifies task-solution generation and harness editing in an agentic reinforcement-learning process, co-evolving model weights, harness components, and solutions [Luo et al., 2026]. TTHE shares the executable-program optimization target but keeps the solver, proposers, and judge frozen, and excludes final correctness feedback from both current-batch program revision and commitment.

Transfer and reliable adoption. Beyond aggregate performance, recent work examines what evolved harnesses retain and when their updates can be trusted. One Recipe, Many Harnesses analyzes artifacts produced by a common evolution recipe across languages and models, distinguishing transferable strategies from ecosystem-specific adaptations [Yang et al., 2026]. A theory of reliable harness self-evolution studies adoption conditions that balance gains on failed tasks against preservation of successful behavior, together with the limits imposed by verification and evaluation costs [Cai et al., 2026b]. TTHE's transfer experiments instead execute batch-specific evolved programs with other backbones. Its conditional analysis concerns a class of trace-triggered edits under a fixed execution coupling.

Self-directed model adaptation. Self-improvement can also change the model itself. STaR bootstraps reasoning by fine-tuning on generated rationales that lead to correct answers [Zelikman et al., 2022]; related work fine-tunes on high-confidence solutions generated from unlabeled questions [Huang et al., 2023]. SEAL learns to generate its own adaptation data and update directives, using post-update performance to train the self-editing policy [Zweiger et al., 2026]. AgentEvolver combines self-generated tasks, experience-guided exploration, and trajectory-level credit assignment to improve agent reinforcement learning [Zhai et al., 2025]. These approaches use experience to improve parameterized capabilities or the process that trains them. In TTHE, experience instead changes the executable procedure through which an unchanged model acquires context, uses tools, verifies results, and recovers from failures.

Test-time adaptation and reinforcement learning. TTT, Tent, and MEMO adapt model parameters or normalization statistics using self-supervised, confidence-based, or augmentation-based objectives on unlabeled test inputs [Sun et al., 2020, Wang et al., 2021, Zhang et al., 2022]. For language-model reasoning, TTRL performs reinforcement learning directly on unlabeled test data, estimating rewards from agreement with majority-voted model outputs [Zuo et al., 2026]. It therefore shares the absence of ground-truth answers during adaptation, but uses the inferred rewards to update model weights. TTC-RL constructs test-time curricula from an available training pool for targeted reinforcement learning [Hübotter et al., 2025], while TTT-Discover trains on experience from a particular test problem, using continuous rewards to prioritize exceptional solutions [Yuksekgonul et al., 2026]. These studies establish test-time learning as more than repeated inference. TTHE pursues a different adaptation state: the model remains fixed, while execution evidence informs program updates and candidate selection without being reduced to a scalar training objective.

Test-time memory and context evolution. Parameter-free adaptation is also studied through persistent memory and evolving contexts. Dynamic Cheatsheet maintains a self-curated memory of strategies, code snippets, and reusable insights at inference time without explicit ground-truth labels [Suzgun et al., 2026]. ACE treats contexts as evolving playbooks, using generation, reflection, and curation with incremental updates; it supports both offline context optimization and online adaptation from execution feedback [Zhang et al., 2026b]. EvoTest evolves prompts, memory, hyperparameters, and executable state-extraction logic across interactive episodes, using transcripts for updates and environment-score statistics for candidate selection [He et al., 2025]. These methods already demonstrate experience accumulation beyond an isolated answer. TTHE focuses on revising the task's control program and committing a single harness whose cached outcomes are scored on the same batch, with final evaluation feedback excluded from the adaptation loop.

Response refinement and execution feedback. Chain-of-thought, self-consistency, and ReAct organize reasoning and tool use within an inference procedure [Wei et al., 2022, Wang et al., 2023, Yao et al., 2023]. Self-debugging and Self-Refine revise candidate answers [Chen et al., 2024, Madaan et al., 2023], and Reflexion retains textual experience for later attempts [Shinn et al., 2023]. Domain-specific systems incorporate these ideas into fixed procedures: DIN-SQL and DAIL-SQL use structured prompting and execution-related processing for text-to-SQL [Pourreza andRafiei, 2023, Gao et al., 2023], while code-generation systems use tests to select candidate solutions [Chen et al., 2022, Li et al., 2022]. Learned verifiers and LLM judges provide further evaluation signals [Lightman et al., 2024, Zheng et al., 2023]. TTHE can express verification and repair within a harness, but adapts the program that specifies when and how these operations occur, rather than only revising a particular response.

sections.heading: E CROSS-DATABASE TRANSFER AND CONTINUED ADAPTATION
sections.text:
TTHE targets adaptation to the current unlabeled batch. As a complementary evaluation, we examine whether an evolved harness transfers to databases excluded from its adaptation stage, and whether continued adaptation yields further gains on the target batches.

Setup and protocol. We partition the baseline-screened genuine hard50 subset of BIRD Mini-Dev [Li et al., 2023] by database, preserving the original question order within each split. The ID split contains 30 questions from card games, formula 1, and toxicology; the OOD split contains 20 questions from california schools, superhero, debit card specializing, and student club. Here, OOD denotes database-disjoint transfer within the same screened benchmark subset.

Starting from the bare text-to-SQL harness, TTHE evolves on the ID split. The final ID harness is frozen before exposure to any OOD questions or evaluation scores. We evaluate this fixed program on both splits without further evolution. Separately, we initialize TTHE with the frozen ID harness and continue adaptation on two OOD batches, scoring each batch with its corresponding committed harness.

All runs use deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash with temperature 0, reasoning enabled, and two workers. TTHE uses batch size B = 10, G = 3 branches, and at most R = 3 rounds. Solver and proposer timeouts are 180 and 2700 seconds, respectively. Results and interpretation. The frozen ID harness achieves 10/30 on the ID adaptation set, compared with 5/30 for the bare baseline (Table 9). More importantly, it achieves 10/20 on the held-out databases without further evolution, versus 2/20 for the baseline. This improvement provides evidence that the evolved task-solving procedure remains useful beyond the databases that supplied its adaptation traces.

Continuing TTHE on the OOD split raises accuracy to 13/20, with 8/10 and 5/10 on the two successive batches. The frozen-transfer result measures reuse without target-side harness evolution, whereas the continuedadaptation result measures the additional benefit of updating the procedure using target-batch execution evidence. Together, these results support both cross-database reuse of an evolved harness and its capacity for further test-time adaptation.

Coupling and a prefix-preserving repair. The error rates e, e ′ and their difference depend only on the prescribed marginals, whereas r, u and ε can depend on κ. For example, let H ′ = H, set D = 0, and suppose the program returns either of two outcomes with equal probability. Sharing its random draw gives ε = 0; independent draws give ε = 1/2, although ∆ X = 0 in both comparisons. Thus ε is not an intrinsic distance between source programs.

For the gated structure illustrated in the main text, couple the child and parent by sharing the unchanged parent execution, including its trace and random draws. The child returns its outcome when D = 0 and invokes repair with fresh randomness when D = 1. This coupling has the required marginals only if the child actually implements that prefix-preserving behavior. The check must preserve all score-relevant untriggered outcomes. Probes and repairs must not change the target, interfere with other instances, or consume resources that alter untriggered behavior. Adding an if statement alone does not establish these properties. No independence between the two executions is required.

Cached outcomes and adaptive selection. Construction may use the same batch, but the realized rollouts in z are distinct from the fresh execution laws above. Conditioning on a program chosen using those rollouts need not preserve their original sampling law. One can also decompose correctness transitions in fixed cached outcomes by averaging over batch indices, but that is an empirical identity for those outcomes, not a guarantee for fresh executions or the adaptive selection process. The results here neither rank candidates from unlabeled evidence nor ensure that the proposer or judge returns a pair satisfying the stated conditions.

sections.heading: F.4 Interpretation and Application Boundaries
sections.text:
Failure soundness is one-sided. A sound rejection flags a final outcome that cannot satisfy the task. Acceptance need not imply correctness. A runtime failure is sound rejection only when it invalidates the submitted outcome under the specified environment. Visible tests qualify only when they are authoritative necessary conditions; noisy, stale, unrelated, or flaky tests do not automatically qualify. A correct SQL query may return zero rows, and an intermediate exception may be recovered from before a correct outcome is submitted. Such signals require potentially imperfect precision π, rather than being classified as sound by default.
